utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. There being no preliminaries, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Lee.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The two documents that you mentioned yesterday. I believe they are D349 and D353. We do not object to those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D349 and D353 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination. You indicated that you would need half an hour, Mr. Stojanovic. Is that still the case? Yes, apparently it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let me remind you that yesterday we left it off with Konjevic Polje 1 and 2. P2086 is the document that I would like us to look at again. This is your report. I'm interested in page 24. There is a reference to the Konjevic Polje 1 graveyard. This is on the English page 23. I would like to call that up. I will invite your comments on the penultimate paragraph on this page. In this paragraph you say that some, if not all, the bodies were picked up by a machine from a different location and put in the graveyard. So in this paragraph you say: "The presence of a non-indigenous white powder (possibly lime) suggested that it must have been placed in the grave." I would like to ask you if you carried out any analysis of that white powder to find out where it had come from and ended up in the Konjevic Polje 1 graveyard.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We collected the white powder, as in other occasions. We have not been personally responsible for the analysis of the white powder. The white powder was given as any other evidence collected from the grave to the scene-of-crime officer. I may remind you, as well, that white powder, such as this one, that apparently was like lime, that's what it looked like, has been found in other sites as well. I think at the Glogova site we have a similar thing and as a matter of fact in a bag -- I mean, as -- a broken bag, as it was thrown from a bag into the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would the presence of lime suggest that the area was disinfected at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lime is used with the belief that it quenches the smell of rotting bodies, and that may cause, as a matter of fact, some disinfection. But this is just popular lore. I mean, it has nothing to do with that. Lime definitely can destroy bodies by burning them -- burning them, pretty much. I mean, it doesn't combust them with fire, but there's a burning element to it. And it is commonly used, as a matter of fact, as I said, to try to destroy the smell. It is nothing to do with disinfection. What it actually does -- what actually happens is that lime becomes a solid crust over the bodies and the bodies underneath may be more preserved through a number of processes, but let's just imagine for the sake of simplicity that lime becomes a solid crust and bodies underneath could be more preserved. From the outside, it may be that they don't smell as much as if the lime wasn't there, but the real -- I mean, the real use of lime in this context is pretty much more a -- something of burning and consuming remains, if it is active lime of course, than anything else. And I think that it would be quick lime, that would be the technical term in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps consider the possibility that the lime may have been used to sanitise the area and to sanitise the grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, as I told you, in my own experience lime is used as an accelerator to destroy remains and probably people, at least in my part of the world, use it, believing that bodies will smell less, not necessarily as a sanitising element, but just something to quench a smell. That's how people use it. But, I mean, no, I did not really think of that possibility of sanitising, more about the smell more than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now let's look at page 6 in the same document, both in English and in B/C/S. Professor, I'd like to deal with Glogova 2 now. Will we agree that that is one of the primary graves that have been identified and that is -- it is close to the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. I'm interested in page 6 in both versions. My question is this: Is this one of the primary mass graves that have been identified and that it is close to the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road? Will you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, there's some primary graves found in that location, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told at any point in time or did you yourself analyse the locations where the people who were eventually buried in the Glogova 2 grave got killed or was it perhaps not your task at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was not, I mean, informed of those details. I do now know, obviously many, many years after, the relationships between Glogova and other sites, but at the time I did not know much. I just knew that there was some graves in the area and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I'll ask you this: Again we come across the information that we can see in the central part of the page in the third paragraph from the top of the page that on one body a watch was found and that it still showed the date as being the 15th of the month. Is that similar to the cases you described yesterday, that you came across such situations in different locations as well, the date showing as being the 15th or the Friday of a certain month?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it is true; however, I would like to point to the fact that in the same report, a few pages ahead, you will find that some other watches were found in the same site with a combination of day and date being Saturday, the 15th. So both, I mean, days occurred, but the same date did occur as well in the same site and in some cases the same brand of watches, they were Seiko, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Professor. There are such reports as well. We're talking about one of the graves that you worked on. What I would like to know from the point of view of your profession can be found in the following paragraph. There you say that: "The graves continued [as interpreted] 73 complete or almost complete bodies and a number of body parts. Most bodies had multiple fractured bones and some of the lower or upper limbs were missing." From the point of view of the rules of your profession, what weapons should have been used in order to inflict such wounds and injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, from the standpoint of my profession and looking back at these remains -- because that is not in the report, because I didn't venture in the report about the mechanism or causing agent of the injuries, I would say that those type of injuries are consistent with blast injuries, I mean, some explosive device of any kind. That is pretty much the only one that can cause these amputations, if you wish, traumatic amputation of limbs or shattering of limbs in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could those have been anti-infantry mines, perhaps, trip-wire mines or similar types of explosives or weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I refer to blast injuries, of course I'm referring to a range of causing agents, I mean, among which could be grenades, could be mines and other type of devices. However, I mean, it would be too speculative if I was to decide that one specific type of device would have been responsible for these type of injuries since I'm not looking at the individual reports. What I do remember, however, from this report is that some of the limbs that were amputated, I'm speaking into quotes here because this was not a surgical amputation, were also charred, were also burned. And the burning episode took place after the fractures were caused. So it is not simply blast, there's an element of blast and there's an element of fire as well that may or may not be related to the blasting episode. So I'm not implying here necessarily that there was something that blasted remains and burned remains. That could have been blast on one end and fire on the other one. So I would say yes to your answer [sic], but I mean it's not a simple yes. It's a yes with consequences, so to speak. I mean, I do not have the reports of the individual remains, but "blast" is a very broad term certainly and I'm speaking here as a very general mechanism. There could be blast, there could be gun-shot, but again I'm not referring in the case of gun-shot where there was a hand-gun or a rifle or anything else. So "blast" would be the generic mechanism in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I'm a bit confused. The question was about the line where it reads: "Most bodies had multiple fractured bones and some of the lower or upper limbs missing." Your explanation, as far as I understood it, was mainly about what could have caused limbs missing. It was not that much about multiple fractured bones. How do I have to understand your answer? That your very cautious provisional conclusions that it most likely is a blast, would that apply to both the multiple fractured bones and the cases where limbs were missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the way. Because there is a -- there is a relationship between the fact there were multiple fractured bones and limbs missing, and in the case of the limbs missing and that what I do remember is you got, for example, a piece of an arm and the rest of the arm was gone, but the piece was totally fractured and charred. So the causative agent was in relationship to the fracturing and the absence of the remains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and fracturing bones as a result of transporting with heavy machinery, is that an issue you considered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, from the experience of previous sites and where -- secondary sites where remains have been broken by machines, that is a type of a very slow velocity blunt force, I mean caused by a machine. High-velocity blunt force caused, for example, by a blast -- that would be one of the mechanism is totally different. You have much more fractures -- radiating fractures and all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you spoke about the subsequent information that you got. Did you learn that this grave, Glogova 2, was somehow associated with the developments in and around the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in the following paragraph it says that the remains were in clay soil rich in vegetation. The clay soil was foreign to the grave and was deposited together with the bodies. During your work, were you able to find a site that may have corresponded with the structure of the soil that was found in the grave, meaning the clay that was found in the grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have not mistaken. Dr. Brown prepared a report on the soil, on this foreign soil, and concluded that the foreign soil -- and my apologies, but I believe that is in the report but I'm just speaking here of what I remember, was consistent with some type of meadow type of soil that has been -- where they have been growing maize. That is what I recall from it. But there was a soil analysis made on the sediment by Dr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, Professor, when it comes to clay, did it appear or was it found in and around the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any -- I mean, any idea regarding that. I can tell you about the clay that was found in the grave. I mean, I have not been, let's say, digging in Kravica, I mean, warehouse. I visited the place many years after, but has no relationship with this in terms of doing a forensic examination of the warehouse, as it were. The clay, I repeat, was found with the bodies in the grave and was obviously foreign to the sediment in which the graves were dug in the first place to collect or to put the bodies inside. So the bodies came with clay. That is a conclusion from the examination of the site. The clay was consistent to have been in an area where maize was grown and was foreign to the specific area where the grave was placed. The relationship within Kravica, the maize, and the clay is something else that I have not personally, I mean, carried out as an investigation. I do have, however, the results of Dr. Brown that were used to substantiate the fact of the maize and the clay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, again, you cannot say anything about the moment when those people died?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we have discussed this issue many times now. I mean, it is not possible from a cursory look at the remains to say whether they died two days ago or three days ago, I mean, a year ago and a year and a half ago, or anything as detailed as that. We are not dealing with a recent crime scene where you do have, let's say, a cadaver on the surface that you can use a number of elements to date it. However, relative dating in this case is primarily carried out through associations of a number of elements. For example, ID cards that were found -- which names were found in the ICRC "Book of the Missing" with dates of disappearance, if I'm not mistaken, yet again that is in the report, between the 11th and the 15th of July, 1995. So that is called relative dating in archaeology as a matter of fact and would be a common tool to establish a relative date, as I'm indicating. So you would say that individuals could not have gone missing after 15th of July because the names were listed as seen last 15th of July. So -- but to answer your question again, no. Through a cursory look it is not possible to say these people died, I don't know, Friday or Thursday or Wednesday. Obviously that wouldn't be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And now let us look at P2090. I am interested in page 7 in B/C/S and in page 11 in the English version. Professor, we're talking about the summary of the report on the excavations at the Zeleni Jadar 6 location. And you are here referring to this as one of the ways used to determine the approximate time of death of those people, something that you also used in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do remember that I believe anyway in the report we have been talking about time of death. We have been saying that people would have been buried about this or that time. Regarding the watches, we refer specifically to the term "death" primarily of the isolation of the wrist based on Mr. Mills' report, but it is correct to say that any identification or document that would have been found in the grave would have been cross-matched with the ICRC "Book of the Missing." And if this person was found in the ICRC "Book of the Missing," this book contains information on when and where this person was last seen and that information would be used to establish this relative dating or to establish the relative chronology of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that would be this example that you cited here and you mentioned a name, where you found the details and in the database you received information that the man was last seen alive on 12th of July, 1995, in Baljkovica, Zvornik municipality. If I tell you that Baljkovica is at least 50 kilometres from Zeleni Jadar, was a geographic analysis included in your investigation? How come that somebody who was seen at Baljkovica on the 12th of July could be found, that is, his body could be found, in the secondary grave of Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do remember that Zeleni Jadar, if I'm not mistaken, was a site or was a secondary site related to one of the Glogova sites, meaning the primary remains came or would have come from Glogova, then been robbed from Glogova, and ended up in Zeleni Jadar. So it is obvious that this person -- actually this person was buried originally in the Glogova site and from there was taken to Zeleni Jadar. I do not know how many kilometres there are between Zvornik municipality or the village you referred to and Zeleni -- and Glogova for that matter, but obviously the logic would be different. I mean, if this is a secondary site, the remains would come from one place to the other. And finally, I mean, I cannot provide you an explanation on how this person travelled from 50 kilometres from one location to the other. I mean, that would totally escape my expertise. I could, I mean, give you various possibilities, but, I mean, I don't think they would have any interest in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I will finish with a short question regarding the grave Ravnice 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask for 52088, page 14 in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you, considering that this analysis is in your report from February 2001, but I understood that you actually never visited this location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether Ravnice 1 is considered to be a primary or a secondary grave according to the standards you adopted?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I couldn't tell you right now. Remember that Ravnice at the time was a site that, if I'm not mistaken, had been subject of a preliminary investigation. So I got only the remains. I did not -- I mean, I didn't have any more information. And this happened in 2000 -- at the end of 2000, meaning when I returned from Kosovo to Bosnia and continued with the laboratory work there. So, I mean, at that time what I do remember is that Ravnice was only preliminary exhumation and I think that they have dug part of it or something of the kind. I do not have much detail. So what I'm reporting here are the results of the examination of the remains without any further information. So -- and even now I wouldn't know whether Ravnice was linked to another site, with a primary or a secondary site, I wouldn't know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, did you ask for 52088 or for P2088?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. P52088. P52088, and I asked for page 14 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that an exhibit number? We are not -- luckily enough, we are not yet in the 52.000s.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2088.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 14 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask regarding this analysis, did you have any information that Ravnice 1 grave is a surface grave?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the structure of the mortal remains, were you able to establish whether these bodies had been in the ground deeper or on the surface?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no difference, as far as I recall, between these bodies and other bodies regarding -- I mean, there was no specific characteristics of these bodies that would have been as important as to put them in the report. But do remember, this is only a preliminary report on the anthropological examination. So if there was any other features of interest, we would need to find them in the pathologist's report. There is only the age distribution and sex distribution of the remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will end with this question: After the advances made in DNA analysis, would the methodological approach we discussed yesterday concerning the -- establishing the lowest, minimum, number of persons become pointless if we have a good DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't because of a -- I mean, of a very simple reason. DNA analysis, no matter how available it is and mechanised, because right now you can work with robots and all sorts of things, still needs a basis to exist, so to speak. DNA analysis is a complementary, very important complementary element to any other kind of analysis. So how would you go about DNA analysis if you don't even know how many people you have or you may have? For some people, the way to go could be, for example, to sample everything. That would be an alternative, of course. I mean, you would go to a grave and just simply rather than counting anything, you would cut a piece of each of the remains, send them for analysis, and then try to find out, to establish, relationships. But I give you an example, let's imagine for a moment that in a grave you find hundreds, if not thousands, of bits and pieces of people, what would be easier to begin with, to determine how many people you have at least represented there and then try to re-associate some parts, or simply in this case to sample every single piece and try to re-associate everything, assuming there are some pieces that may not provide DNA. So you may have, for example, I don't know, a foot, are you going to take a piece of the foot and you won't get any DNA. So you still have a foot that you cannot associate to anybody. So in my humble opinion, I would say that this type of approach, the MNI, in that respect is, I mean, totally, totally valid. It is a starting point; it is not the end point. It is a starting point of any investigation. It's just pure logical, I mean, work. I mean, it's not old-fashioned, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let me conclude. According to the rules of your profession, are you able to rule out the possibility that the bodies of a certain number of persons killed in combat were brought to the so-called primary graves and buried there together with the bodies of persons who were unlawfully executed?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it is very clear that some graves contain people that died at least in special circumstances. One of them would be the Glogova graves that we referred to a moment ago regarding blast injuries, for example, as compared to other graves where people died of gun-shot wounds. It is not my role, of course, to qualify whether blast injuries account for casualties in combat, nor whether gun-shot injuries account for the same. What remains very clear is that in some occasions there were people that were shot while lying in the grave, and that by definition, in my opinion, would exclude the possibility of combat inasmuch as somebody is lying in a grave, and if there is a grave the intention is to bury somebody. That would be the logic of events. Now, as a possibility - and what you're proposing is a possibility - I would say that everything is possible but not everything is probable. I mean, of course it is possible, but every single thing in this planet is possible 50/50. So that bodies in some occasions could have been brought in from elsewhere or from a battle or something. It is possible. None of the things I have related in this report, however, point to the fact at -- specifically at this. I would say the opposite. If this was the case, why there would have been so much investment of time and energy to destroy some of the sites? That's something I can still not understand. My report discusses at length the attempts of individuals to rob these sites with machines and excavators and all the rest of it and create these secondary graves, and that for me, yet again in my opinion, has to do more with concealment and destruction than anything else. If all the graves were graves of people that died in combat and have been just disposed there for humanitarian reasons, there would have been no reason to go back and destroy them. But obviously this is just my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree that this is an opinion which is not a result of your science but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first of all, the witness explained that. Second, you have now put your third final question to the witness. I think the witness has been very clear that this was his personal opinion and -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank the expert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, any questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: May I have P2086 back on the screen. And may I have page 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, if you look at the first paragraph, and today you spoke about Dr. Brown's report in relation to the Glogova 2 site, and you referred to Dr. Brown's report and the analysis of soil and it says "Brown 1999a."

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And may I have now, please, P -- I'm sorry, page 43 of the same report.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: The first item, 1999a, is that what you were citing in your report earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now may I please have 65 ter number 04503.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: In that report -- I'm sorry, before we go there, the first item it says statement to the ICTY and then it's dated the 29th of November, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I apologise. May I please have 65 ter number 04503, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Now this report is -- appears to be Dr. Brown's report from 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: And now may I please have page 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, is this the report that you're referring to when you spoke about the soil analysis containing maize in Glogova site?

utterances.speaker: JOSE BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please -- I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood correctly, that's the entire expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What it is, Mr. Stojanovic, is a five-page document, so the entire report is -- it is a statement of witness, it says. And it refers to reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: It refers to the Glogova evidence and the Nova Kasaba site. And these -- this is a report that had been -- the witness was asked questions about this area and the witness says that he relied on this report. And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a factual basis. Is there any dispute about the existence of such a report in which this conclusion appears?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no dispute about this report, but from the methodological point of view, this kind of tendering is something you told us could not be acceptable in terms of 92 bis or 92 ter. This would then be the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Lee, a statement taken for the purposes of this Tribunal, that seems to be not a methodological, but, I would rather say, a procedural issue raised by Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I understand that, but this -- on this page specifically it refers to Glogova but it also refers to Zeleni Jadar and the link between the two, and that is something that had been challenged during cross-examination. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- just one clarification. What is in dispute - and you saw this through questions - is not whether Glogova was a primary site and Zeleni Jadar secondary. What is in dispute is Kravica as the site of execution and the link with Glogova. But there is nothing, not a single word, in this report about this link. And at any rate, the statement should not be tendered or admitted in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever it refers to, Ms. Lee, doesn't change Rule 92 ter, would it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is more of a report and not a -- this is not the same ICTY-type of witness statements that we received. This is Dr. Brown's report. It's been referred to as report and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do we deal with reports under the Rules? It seems to be pretty much -- at least it has the appearance of containing some expert knowledge in reports. What is the usual way of dealing with expertise as contained in reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Well, this is a report that was -- we are not calling Dr. Brown as a 94 [sic] bis witness, Your Honour. However, this is a report that this witness has testified about, that he has referred to, and it relates to a matter that has been challenged by the Defence in relation to the maize --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What -- the reference I think was - and that's what you pointed at as well - was that -- that's how I think the witness dealt with it. It's about conclusion number 3: "The GL03 matrix is from an open environment, probably a meadow which has in the past been used under cereal cultivation including maize ... cultivation (probably the previous season)." I think that is the only reference the witness made to this report of Dr. Brown, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Yes, and we've heard evidence about Sandici meadow in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but again you go to the substance. I'm still there with procedure. The witness referred as a basis for his answer to what he says he read in a report by Dr. Brown. Is there any dispute about what I just read being in the report of Dr. Brown? Because if not, then I think the witness -- the reference of the witness to the factual basis for what he further elaborated on seems not to be in dispute. If you do dispute it, then -- Mr. Stojanovic, what I just read, any dispute that that's part of -- that that is found in Dr. Brown's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That part is not in dispute. It is there and it relates to the link between Glogova and Zeleni Jadar, not Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the parties agree on at least what the reference about the -- what Dr. Brown found in relation to ground which would have been used to cultivate maize.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider it, but we would like to re-read exactly the context in which the matter was raised by Mr. Stojanovic and the maize and distance and -- before we decide. But at least it is on the record that where the witness referred to a finding of Dr. Brown, that the parties agree that such a finding by Dr. Brown appears in the report as I just read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions? You don't have to invent them now but --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I will not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if there were any --

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I don't. But if you could just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LEE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then we are close to the time for a break. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the witness is about to leave, we would like to re-read the transcript right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness on page 8 in his answer referred to a report of Dr. Brown about the analysis of the soil and he mentioned growing maize in this respect, and there seems to be no dispute between the parties that such a report does exist and that the recollection of the witness, therefore, accurately reflects what is in that report. Under those circumstances, the Chamber denies admission into evidence of the report itself because it would have required a -- either a 92 bis, 92 ter, or an expert report treatment before we could admit it. The report is made for the specific purposes of this Tribunal. Then, Mr. Baraybar, this -- but I first have to ask Mr. Stojanovic whether he has any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither have my colleagues. Therefore this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that both the parties and the Bench have put to you and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break of 20 minutes. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00 and then the Prosecution will call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the next witness to be called would be Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will already ask him to be escorted into the courtroom, unless there's any reason why we should delay that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just getting settled so I can hear things and get back to this courtroom. It's been a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could Mr. Butler be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, everyone. I -- you will have seen I requested an estimate of ten hours for Mr. Butler, and I have made every effort to try to make this as targeted and narrow as possible. It's much, much shorter than I have done in the past, but I do encourage you to ask questions because I may be jumping to places where I may have spent more detail before, though I'm confident we can get through this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Time estimates, Mr. McCloskey, are a difficult matter, I'm aware of that, especially if it goes beyond two or three hours you're encouraged to reduce but at least stick to it. And don't hesitate -- don't worry about the Judges asking questions. You may have, by now, gained the experience that we do if we think that there's something relevant to be asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I know I don't really have to encourage you, but I just -- I welcome them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler, I take it. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler. Please be seated. Mr. Butler, you'll first be examined by Mr. McCloskey. I don't have to tell you that you find him to your right because you know him. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you state your name, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, my name is Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your -- I'm reminding myself to pause, as I remind you, Mr. Butler. What is your current position and job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I am an intelligence research specialist, in my case the intelligence operations manager, for the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Centre, which is a component of the United States Department of Homeland Security, US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 26039.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be your CV. How long have you worked for the Federal Government? I'm not including the United States Army in that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I departed the Tribunal in November of 2003. I became employed by the United States Federal Government in February of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see from the first page of your CV that it's dated 10 June 2011. Anything major to add in terms of different work from June 2011 to today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly a little bit about that work that you do for the Department of Homeland Security.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: To a large degree, it is a similar type of work that I used to do for the Tribunal here. In this particular instance, I both do my own individual analysis as well as I manage an analytical team that supports domestic investigations by the United States Government into individuals who have committed human rights violations abroad and whom we now determine are within the jurisdiction of the United States for either criminal prosecution purposes or immigration purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you said who have committed but are suspected of having committed, is that what you intended to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some cases there are individuals again suspected of having committed human rights violations. In some cases there are individuals who have been charged or even convicted in absentia and who have fled to the United States in order to avoid sentence or other things abroad so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say for criminal prosecution those are the suspects and for the other category it may be that they have been convicted already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in that capacity, do you work with federal investigators and prosecutors and sometimes testify in prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, your job before the Federal Government, as you noted, was with the Office of the Prosecutor here at the ICTY. And how many years did you work here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was with the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY from April of 1997 to November of 2003, so that's almost seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll get into that in a bit of detail, but what I'm going to ask you now about is your career in the United States Army. As we can see from your CV, you've been an intelligence officer, it looks like, the majority of the time. Can you tell us when you enlisted in the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That would be back in August of 1981, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that out of high school or secondary school?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It was approximately two years after high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you become an intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I spent the first roughly seven years of my military career as first an enlisted soldier and then as a non-commissioned officer in the intelligence field. And in 1988 I was appointed as a warrant officer in the United States Army, again in the intelligence field and ultimately was commissioned in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Describe again briefly your advancement through the intelligence field.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, as an enlisted soldier and non-commissioned officer, I had a variety of jobs at various military units where I learned how to conduct various forms of intelligence work. My primary career field was that of an analyst. So it was during those years at a number of assignments, some of them strategic assignments with the military intelligence group, some of them tactical assignments with combat formations, that I essentially learned my trade of how to conduct intelligence work in support of military commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see from your CV that just prior to coming here you describe your job as an all-source intelligence technician. Can you give us the guts of what kind of work you do for your superiors, what kind of material you analysed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In 1988, again, I was appointed as a warrant officer. In the United States military, warrant officers are considered to be the technical experts of a various branch in a variety of fields. In my case as an intelligence officer, intelligence warrant officer, I was the technical expert in the field of intelligence. I continued to apply my trade with respect to intelligence collection and analysis as an expert at higher levels, at division, at corps, and at army levels in positions of greater and greater responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you -- and I know we can't get into the details of your work in any combat zones, but have you worked in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I've worked in a combat environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what kind of materials you were able to review as an intelligence officer and analyse and did it have anything similar to what you ended up looking at here in brief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the field of intelligence and analysis work, it is broken up into several disciplines of intelligence. They're most broadly referred to as HUMINT or human intelligence, which is various forms of intelligence and information derived from human sources. That would include things, for example, like the interview of individuals, refugees, prisoners of war, line-crossers, things of that nature. It would include the debriefing of clandestine sources of information that are collected from other humans. It would include -- under that genre we also include document exploitation, which would be the review and analysis of captured military documents, map products, things of that nature. It also includes what we call open-source exploitation, which is the review of not necessarily classified but other important documents that might be -- one might be able to derive intelligence value from, such as military magazines, such as articles pertaining to various military forces by outside experts. The second major discipline is known as SIGINT or signals intelligence and it is the classical use of information that is derived from an adversary's electronic use of media. In a technical sense, it is the intercepting of an enemy combatant's radio communications. It would include the intercept or the exploitation of even non-communications emitters, such as radars. Today, as many people are obviously becoming aware, it includes things such as potentially computers and the internet. So it is a broad field with respect to signals intelligence and communication intelligence. The third of the fields is imagery intelligence or IMINT as it's called, and that is the exploitation of imagery-related products for the ability to derive intelligence information from them. Those could include things such as photographs taken from ground level. It would include aerial imagery. It would include digital imagery. So again, a variety of information sources that as an all-source intelligence technician I was required to be proficient in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would you be -- would the rules of an enemy or an army related to their internal processes or their external or their laws be anything that you would be interested in or did you leave that to others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. That would obviously be something that as a professional military analyst I'm interested in. My role at the end of the day in support of my commanders is to be able to advise them on what a potential armed adversary is doing and to assist them in essentially their goal, which is defeating an armed adversary. For me to do that, I obviously have to be able to understand, to the maximum degree possible, the ability of that enemy or armed adversary as they operate on a modern battle-field. That would include, for example, understanding how their command and control functioned. It would include, for example, understanding the professional military background of their key commanders. It would matter that I understood how military forces supplied themselves with food, with fuel, with ammunition, and other technical services, all of those things that if my military force that I work for could understand and attack, it would degrade their capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How would you communicate your analysis, your views, to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It would depend primarily on the circumstances at the time. If I were an intelligence professional at a small unit that was immediately and decisively engaged in combat operations, most of my analysis and findings would be obviously oral in nature or very sketchy written products that could be quickly put together. When I was in assignments that allowed for time to create detailed analytical products and reports, that is how I answered those requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me -- can you clarify what you meant by the American slang "sketchy."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, it's not an issue of the quality of the work. It's an issue of the time involved. There's just not time at certain places and certain locations to get into a great amount of details. So you had to be obviously aware of how much time that you had with your commander to be able to get him the most pertinent and salient facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I want you to be able to tell us a bit how what you've just described as your work for the United States Army, how -- if that had -- was similar to the work you did here. But first, when you first came on to the Office of the Prosecutor, were you employed by the United Nations or by the United States Army and how did that work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At that time I was not a United Nations member. I was still a warrant officer in the United States Army. I was seconded to the US Department of State, which in turn loaned me to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY. So again, I was, for official purposes, seconded by the United States Government to the Office of the Prosecutor. And I remained in that status for five years. When I retired from the United States Army in 2001, the United Nations then signed me to one of their standard United Nations civil servant contracts. So for my last two years in The Hague, I was a United Nations civil servant or a UN employee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the majority of your time at the OTP, did you work for one investigation in particular?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I arrived in April of 1997, and if I recall correctly, in June of 1997 I was assigned to support Srebrenica investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So for those several years that you worked in support of the Srebrenica investigation, can you again briefly outline for us the kind of work you did, especially as it related to the kind of work you just described that you did for the United States Army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of my early requirements placed on me by the investigators who were looking at Srebrenica was to try and gain an understanding of at that time, you know, what was the Drina Corps as an entity because from the investigation they were already deriving evidence that suggested that elements of the Drina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska might have some involvement in the larger crimes. So as the first component of my work, first it was understanding how the Army of the Republika Srpska worked and how it was organised in July of 1995, and I approached that in much the same manner that I would and did in the United States Army against other adversaries. Using the rules and regulations of the former JNA, which had been translated, I studied those rules and regulations to determine if the Army of the Republika Srpska was still following those rules and regulations and the associated operating practices. I then started to look at the few documents that we had at the time that laid out the organisation and structure of the Army of the Republika Srpska as it existed in 1995. In 1998, the Office of the Prosecutor was, you know, conducted a number of searches in the Republika Srpska, two of which were subordinate brigades of the Drina Corps, the Zvornik Brigade and the Bratunac Brigade, and in those searches the Office of the Prosecutor obtained I think approximately 17.000 documents from those units, which greatly advanced my particular knowledge of the organisation of the Drina Corps, the organisation of the various brigades and battalions of the Drina Corps, and how the command relationships worked. At approximately the same time, the Office of the Prosecutor started to obtain what we call intercepts which were -- the intelligence intercepts, the radio intelligence intercepts collected by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that they had collected against the Army of the Republika Srpska during the conflict are particularly in Eastern Bosnia during the month of July in 1995. So I was also able to analyse that material and integrate it into my running analysis as to the involvement of the army, the Drina Corps and subordinate formations, in what would be the Srebrenica 1995 crime base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. Did you take these intercepts at face value or did you look into any reliability issues?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. Clearly with the intercepts being provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by a third party, just like I would with any information being provided by a third party, we were and I was personally very skeptical of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me again interrupt you. This wasn't just any third party, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, it was the other affected party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just who - I think we know that - but can you just identify that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Most of the intercepts came from the radio intelligence collection units of the Bosnian 2nd Corps, which, of course, was directly involved in ground combat against their counterparts of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in your review of that material, did you find it valuable?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Well, ultimately I came to find it valuable because we were able to corroborate much of the information that was contained in those intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I won't get into that. So you've mentioned your review of documents, now intercepts. What else were you able to review as the investigation carried on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As the investigation carried on, particularly at the end of 1998 and during 1999 when it really took off in earnest, the Office of the Prosecutor began to get granted access by the Government of the Republika Srpska to a number of VRS military officers and soldiers who were part of the Drina Corps in July of 1995 as well as other officers of the Main Staff. So once we started having access to those individuals, it was an opportunity there to take my particular analysis of the situation as well as the documents that we had and ask those particular officers what their view of particular documents meant and whether or not, you know -- essentially to determine whether or not the basic analysis that I had accomplished with respect to the rules and applicability of the JNA applying to the VRS during the course of the service, whether those rules had changed, whether they were still following the operating procedures of the former Yugoslav national army even though they were now the new Army of the Republika Srpska. And by and large these officers confirmed that the rules and regulations of the former JNA and the former Soviet -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were still being applied to the VRS in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You mentioned you had access to VRS people or the OTP did. Did that include access to police, MUP, civilians as well to some degree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. With respect to police in the MUP, and of course my particular interest them was as a result of their subordination to the army leadership at the time in July of 1995. I had access to other civilians also, either personally or, you know, participated in interview or statements of certain political officials, but generally my focus was on the military relationships between the army and the police and then their inter-relationships with the political branches, not necessarily the politics in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I take the witness back to one of his previous answers and seek clarification. You were asked, and I read from the transcript: "Did you take these intercepts at face value or did you look into any reliability issues?" The answer then was: "No, sir. Clearly with the intercepts being provided ..." And then you said you were skeptical about the value. Now, first of all, may I take it that "no, sir" is only an answer to the first part of the question, that is, whether you took the matter at face value --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not to whether you looked into reliability issues? Because I do understand the answer there would be "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We spent -- and not only myself but other analysts involved in the team spent several years over the course of working this investigation dealing with the question of the reliability of the intercepts, and again I was obviously part of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So not only you were skeptical, but a lot of time was spent on investigating it. Now, did you ever come across an intercept where you said: Well, this is not reliable to the extent that it would have been a forgery or with wrong dates or -- I mean, because that's -- that's what I would like to know, whether that happened or whether you always found them to reflect what -- what was said at the time reported through the communication as reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When -- when one uses the phrase, when you look at -- looking at the reliability of signal intercept information -- and I have to remind people, and I've testified to this in the past, there are two criteria that you are using. The first one with respect to reliability is from a technical perspective. Does the individual or collection entity actually have the technical ability to collect the information which they are now telling you that they have possession of? And so there was part of the investigation that established that the Bosnian 2 Corps and its associated intelligence elements had the technical ability to collect against the VRS communications, and in this sense they did so reliably. What they heard and what they copied was what ultimately became part of the intercept reports that they provided to their own commanders. The second part of reliability, as one looks at it from an intelligence standpoint, is making a determination as to whether or not the actual information that is contained in the intercept is factual. And there will be I think in some of the exhibits I will discuss, there will be situations where an intercept is factually accurate with respect to what has been heard and transcribed by the operators, but the fact is that the individuals who were communicating back and forth over the telephone do not have an accurate picture of the truth. So you know, in that particular context what I can tell you clearly is that we have been able to establish the reliability of the intercepts, that they're not fraudulent for this case or in the cases that we discuss here. However, there will be times when it will become clear that correspondence in a particular intercept will be discussing a situation but not have an accurate view of what they're discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you never came across any fraudulent writing down what was never heard and what was never said or could not have been intercepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my question. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Related to that, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that misinformation over the airways, deliberate -- sending out deliberate false information, knowing the enemy is listening, is something that armies do. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you come across anything that you believed was misinformation sent out by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did. It was something obviously that I was looking for, it's something that we practice in the US military. Again, it goes back to understanding the purpose of misinformation, and that is in a military environment to draw the attention of, first, the intelligence individuals and then the generals or commanders who you're advising, to draw them away from one part of a battle-field to another during a critical point in time or in an operation. The thing about a misinformation campaign is it can't obviously last for a long time because at some point the intelligence does become aware of what is really happening. So when we talk about, for example, putting together a dummy communications network to allow the enemy to think that another infantry division, for example, is operating in this area, you recognise that at some point in time other forms of intelligence are going to confirm or deny that that division actually exists. So you're trying to buy yourself time for maybe 24 or 48 hours before, for example, you know, a reconnaissance flight goes over and shows an empty desert where there's supposed to be hundreds of tanks. The second part of looking at many of these intercepts is the content of the intercept, is it designed to draw the individual who would be collecting it, in this case the Bosnian Muslim 2nd Corps, away from critical areas of the battle-field. Now, when one looks at the body of intercepts as a whole, it becomes clear that the intercepts that are being collected by the Bosnian Muslims is not, in fact, focusing their attention to other less critical parts of the battle-field. It, in fact, mirrors the communications that the VRS is doing at critical points in time on the battle-field and even with respect to the execution of war crimes in 1995. So, in fact, they're not drawing any attention away from these issues through careless communications security procedures; they're actually focusing the attention of the Army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina 2nd Corps people to those very issues that at other levels they're seeking to avoid attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what your role in the investigation was, in particular you've mentioned a process by which access was gained to VRS officers. Did you play a role in the investigation? Did you play a role in the interviews?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did. Again, just like within the context of my military position, my job was to analyse military-related information and provide that information to the investigators and the prosecutors who were reviewing the actual criminal aspects of what was -- what is now the Srebrenica crime base. Clearly in context, given the suspected heavy involvement of the Drina Corps and the Main Staff and associated RS police units in the conduct of the crime, my work obviously had a big role, I suspect, in helping to focus the investigators and the prosecutors towards the key events as well as allowing them to understand the authorities of the various commanders on the ground who were controlling such events as they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in particular, what was your role in an interview? Why would you go and be involved in an interview?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Many of our investigators did not have prior military service and, of course, were obviously qualified professional criminal investigators, but they were interviewing military officers. Often these officers would explain, as I do, issues in a very technical sense. And as a military professional myself, one of my roles was to then advise the investigator: Here's what he's saying, here's what the individual means by that, as well as to suggest follow-up areas of potential interview to clarify certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And at some point throughout all this investigation and involvement, were you asked to write reports with your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was not asked to write reports per se early on. What I decided based on my previous experience was that, again acknowledging that many of the investigators and legal officers on the investigation team did not have a military background, what I decided to do was create a series of running narratives or reports on various aspects of the Drina Corps, the Main Staff, the various brigades, and the military documents and how they related to events on the ground in July of 1995 so that the investigators and the lawyers would have a running guide to what was happening with respect to the Drina Corps, what the documents meant in context to the events that occurred on the ground back then, who each person was who signed a document, all of those things so they would have a more comprehensive understanding of the military's role with respect to what was happening there in July of 1995. And again, keeping in mind I'm doing all of this years after the actual commission of the crime. It turned out after the indictment of General Krstic, when people started thinking through perhaps the most effective way to explain all of that information to the Trial Chamber in the case of General Krstic, that one of the options that was posed was if we could take these existing narratives that I was drafting and turn them into formal reports that could then potentially be submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor to the Trial Chamber as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you mentioned narratives regarding events and such. Did you separate the report from something you've called a command report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain that. The Trial Chamber has those reports and so we don't -- I don't want to get into great detail, but I do want to understand how you put these together. So what's the difference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The command reports, you know, since we're dealing with generals, colonels, military officers who are operating under the authorities granted to them by their respective states and governments, I felt it would be useful for our investigators and legal professionals to have a listing of all of the various authorities by which these officers operated under law in their own environment. So the command reports essentially lay out four various echelons of command, the types of authorities and responsibilities of these individuals as it occurred under their own rules and regulations; what were the authorities of a brigade commander under VRS procedures and law, under the regulations; who was responsible for appointing these commanders; what were the limits of their authority at various echelons of command. So that was the function of what I call the command responsibility reports, to essentially lay out the regulatory and legal framework of how an individual assumes and functions in a position of command in the Army of the Republika Srpska and what that actually means under their rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so just describe which separate command reports you've drafted. I will offer those into evidence afterwards, but can you -- so we have a clear view of that, what were they entitled, roughly, or what were they about just each one in a sentence or so.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There's one that covers VRS corps-level command. There is one that covers brigade-level command. And there is one report that covers command at the Main Staff level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now the narrative reports, how many narrative reports?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There are two versions of the narrative report: An initial report that was done and submitted as evidence by the Office of the Prosecutor in the Krstic case in 2000; and I subsequently revised and expanded that report in 2002 for use in the Prosecutor's case against Colonel Blagojevic and Major Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in the narrative, as you've described it, did you use and analyse many of the sources of intelligence that you've just described, signal intelligence, documents, and such?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In the narrative report is where I attempt in as much detail as I could possibly do at the time to lay out the military context of what was happening in Eastern Bosnia with respect to Srebrenica in July of 1995 based on my analysis of the military documents and of the intercepts that we had possession of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about human intelligence of -- or the human information from interviews of alleged victim survivors and witnesses, which we all know that there are thousands of such, if not millions of such, interviews, how did you use or not use that kind of material?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As a rule, I did not use that information with respect to witness interviews, interviews of military officers, things of that nature. If there's one artificial aspect to what I've done with the narrative, it is because I also do recognise that this is a judicial process at the end of the day. And knowing that many of those individuals would be called to testify before the Tribunal, it's certainly not my position to endorse or in another manner weigh the accuracy or the credibility of their testimony; that's obviously the Trial Chamber's position. Where I included witness testimony it is primarily for survivors of mass executions and it is only for the limited purpose of setting the context of that event so that the military documents that I have been able to assemble with respect to those things have some form of context and meaning. So, for example, in my report I will go into a very limited discussion of a survivor's account of the Orahovac execution, only for the purpose so that the reader of that report can then understand what engineer documents related to bulldozers at Orahovac meant in context of what was occurring at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would like to now take you through what will -- should be a narrative in some respects, where I will ask you your views on various documents that you have testified about or incorporated about over the years in your reports, trying to get rather quickly to the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could begin that process, the first document I'd like to go to is at P338. And this is called "The Analysis of Combat-Readiness and Activities of the Army of Republika Srpska in 1992." And I'd actually -- I apologise. I would like to offer the CV into evidence as well, 26039.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2094, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2094 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this is dated April 1993. And can you very briefly describe who wrote this, as far as you know, and what is it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Even though the VRS was obviously a relatively young military force in 1992 or 1993 when this report was written, from the origins of the JNA, the officers were obviously well-educated military professionals. One of the things that they recognised is -- as a higher function of military command and staff work is rigorous review and self-analysis of their operations for the purpose of learning lessons and encapsulating those lessons in order to make their operations more effective in the future. This is one of the documents that they produced, an analysis of their own operations and activities in 1992, which I believe they published in April of 1993, is what the date says, out of the Main Staff. So this is their annual evaluation for 1992 which reflects in a short 160-some-odd pages, their own self-criticism of their performance for the first year of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't think we need to go to it, but we can see on page 157 of the English and 137 of the B/C/S that it's actually -- the first part of it is signed off by the Supreme Commander, Radovan Karadzic. And does that change your analysis on who wrote it or why would his name be on this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir. The document was obviously authored by the various individuals of the Main Staff. President Karadzic, as the Commander-in-Chief of the armed forces, it would be appropriate for him -- this report to be presented to him for his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Commander-in-Chief, that's an American term, isn't it? Do you know what the term for the Republika Srpska would be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's alternatively seen in various regulations as -- or laws as either Commander-in-Chief or the Supreme Commander. So in this context it's Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I -- I know this is a subject of your report and others' reports, so I don't want to get into this in much detail, but I do -- would like to ask you about some -- a comment that's on page 9 of the English. It's also B/C/S page 9. And I'll slowly read this as we're coming to that. "We devoted significant attention to controlling and extending assistance to the subordinate commands so that these important activities were carried out on schedule, in accordance with questions settled in advance, and according to regulations. Inspection was carried out by employing the method of team tours, with observations being made on the spot. In most cases, organs of the Main Staff personally corrected mistakes in the Commands immediately. We submitted our observations subsequently, and set them to task of eliminating the observed deficiencies. The involvement of different Main Staff bodies in the brigades and other units yielded particularly good results because in that way directives, commands and orders reached those who were to execute them in the fastest possible way, and the planned concerted action was relatively quickly performed." And this is under the chapter entitled: "Control and Command." You've commented on this before. What is the importance, in your view, of this statement? What does it tell you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: One of the fundamental tenets of command and control is the issuance of orders and the monitoring of the process to ensure that orders are complied with. Military staffs at various levels have a number of ways to ensure that this occurs. One of the more effective ways that a military hierarchy can ensure that commands are followed is through frequent inspection by individuals from the higher-level headquarters to the subordinate formation, to ensure that they receive the orders, to ensure that they are carried out in a timely manner, and most importantly to ensure that the intent behind the order is clearly understood by the subordinate formation and soldiers who would have to carry it out. So the fact that Main Staff inspection teams regularly visited subordinate corps and even beyond that subordinate brigade-level commands to evaluate their processes and to ensure that orders that are being issued at the higher level are being clearly understood and carried out as rapidly and as effectively as possible is a mark of a very mature and well-managed military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go to the -- a section at the end of this document. It should be page 158 in the English, page 138 in the Serbian. And it's in a section called: "Basic Characteristics of the Operational - Tactical Utilisation of the Army of Republika Srpska." And that is signed by a Colonel Dragutin Ilic. And if we could go in particular to page 160 in the English and page 139 in the Serbian, I'd like to read you just a paragraph that's talking about a couple of different regions. The paragraph begins, it's the second paragraph down: "In Posavina and Western Bosnia we have put emphasis on the grouping of forces, air and artillery support ..." So I'm not really asking you about the Posavina or Western Bosnia, but here's the subject of the question: "... and in Podrinje, in a specific way, the increased expenditure of ammunition and materiel and equipment, as well as the use of the reserves of the Main Staff of the Army of the RS. The presence of the commander of the Main Staff, or of a representative of the Main Staff, in the units carrying out the mission of the liberation of Podrinje in a specific way of giving weight to and steering combat operations towards a single goal." Now, can you remind us, Podrinje, what area is that to your understanding?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The Podrinje area, as it's used in the context of the Drina Corps area, is what geographically is the western Drina Valley, keeping in mind that the eastern Drina Valley is in Serbia.
